segments.text: There are hundreds of videos about what a perfect ‘Review meeting’ should be like...
but how about showing you a real one instead, one that took place just a few weeks ago?
I am Bram De Block, Agile coach at Skyline Communications.
But before we jump in. We need some context.
In a review meeting, we inspect the increment
and adapt based on what we discover.
We have all the necessary people participating:
we have the development team, the Agile Coach, the Product Owner,
and most importantly: real end users from YLE.
YLE, the biggest broadcasting company in Finland, who are awesome since
they joined us in this Agile Partnership.
The increment we are going to look at is a new and improved table component YLE wants
to use to create and edit work orders.
And work orders could be anything  like grabbing a live signal from a satellite feed
and transferring it to a news studio   to show a reporter live on scene.
Or... an order could be that a memory card needs to be taken out of a camera and
uploaded to a server. That and everything in between.
Alright, that's enough context.   Let's have a look.
So here the Product Owner is very excited
to show everything the team managed to complete, which is great, but he's forgetting to give
room for the most important thing of  a review meeting: getting feedback!
That's also the biggest difference between a demo and a review meeting.
With a demo you show something and that's it.   DONE. Everybody goes home.
While in a review meeting, the demo is only the beginning  and serves as a trigger for feedback.
Another benefit of a review meeting is providing context to the developers.
And this is context you can only get by putting developers and end users in the same room.
Every day, a developer needs to make hundreds   of decisions during development.
Getting this context from the end user during a review meeting
will help them make INFORMED decisions. Compare that to having to figure out what
the context is simply based on.. what?
Requirements? Made 6 months ago,  written down somewhere?
Guess what … a lot has changed since 6 months ago.
In this next fragment, the development team
decides NOT to implement a feature from the old table component, namely a check mark
in front of a row, because they don't understand its use case.
Can you imagine the amount of time and energy that would have been wasted optimizing
a checkmark feature that is not even going to be used?
An important detail is setting a firm timebox.
The timebox helps everyone involved to focus on what is going to give the best possible outcome
and what prevents the participants from falling down a rabbit hole.
Don't mistake a review meeting for being a good-news show.
More often than not, the most valuable outcome of a review meeting is transparency
that is gained on important things that are still MISSING.
The limit set to the table will break the usability.
See the PO hashing it out? He's thinking. "Ok, so this is much more important than we anticipated,
but what will be the impact on the backlog?"
And THAT is absolutely the goal of a review meeting, not the demo
itself, but giving Product Owners a lot to think about so they can update the product
backlog and maximize value for the next iteration.
So how do you know if the Review wasn't a waste of time? If it was useful for everyone?
You ask.
Having proactive users, like we were lucky to have here with people from YLE, is essential
in creating value. The users ARE the drivers of VALUE.
Without their input, their feedback during regular reviews,
we would only be able  to deliver a fraction of the possible value.
And then I'd like to end by highlighting one last   benefit of a review meeting,
and that's a happy team.
Knowing, seeing, hearing and FEELING
that what you created means something to someone is simply awesome and motivating
That was the end of our Review meeting.  Thanks for watching!
I hope you enjoyed it and find it inspiring.
Feel free to leave a comment and I'll get back to you ASAP.
